item.content:encoded:
A body-language analyst says Trump administration officials appeared stressed and evasive while explaining Friday’s nationwide ground stop, but the supplied reporting does not establish that either official lied—or identify what supposedly remains concealed. Dr. John Paul Garrison’s case rests on lowered eyes, heavy breathing, blinking, facial movements and an awkward exchange between Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Those observations may show discomfort. Calling them signs of deception is an inference, not a finding.

That distinction matters because the ground stop involved federal authority over air travel, and the public explanation reportedly centered on a software problem. The officials responsible for explaining such a sweeping disruption owe the public a coherent account. Yet speculation about their involuntary gestures cannot substitute for testing that account against the system failure, the government’s decisions and the resulting operational consequences.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A press conference read as a confession

AlterNet reports that Garrison, a clinical and forensic psychologist who produces YouTube body-language videos, examined Mullin and Duffy’s appearance at a press conference following the ground stop.

Garrison interpreted Mullin’s conduct as evidence of anxiety. Mullin gripped the microphone stand as though bracing himself, breathed heavily and repeatedly looked away from reporters while trying to dismiss rumors about the software issue. Garrison argued that Mullin’s glance toward reporters after speaking could have been an unconscious attempt to determine whether they believed him.

He also focused on Mullin’s unusually flat delivery. According to Garrison, Mullin ordinarily gestures and uses expressive facial movements for emphasis, making the subdued presentation seem “peculiar.” Both men blinked frequently, which Garrison read as stress.

Duffy appeared more comfortable while discussing technical matters, Garrison said, but his behavior changed when a reporter raised the possibility that routers had been overloaded with data. Garrison interpreted movements Duffy made with his tongue as an effort to “hold something back.”

None of those reactions identifies a false statement. Anxiety can accompany deception, as Garrison suggested, but he also acknowledged that the officials could have been uncomfortable for other reasons. That concession is not incidental. It is the boundary between observing conduct and claiming knowledge of what caused it.

The exchange that deserves scrutiny

The more consequential moment involved what the officials actually said. Mullin began discussing “new patches into the system” and “new equipment,” while Duffy reportedly lowered his head and shook it. Garrison inferred that Duffy wanted Mullin to stop because Mullin was effectively assigning blame to him.

Duffy then turned to funding, arguing that he could not act without money. Garrison characterized that pivot as a distraction from questions about the administration’s explanation and its insistence that the situation was under control.

That exchange raises legitimate questions without requiring anyone to diagnose a blink. Did the failure involve obsolete equipment, inadequate upgrades, overloaded routers or some combination of problems? Were patches or replacement hardware already required? What did Duffy lack the money to do, and who controlled that funding? The officials’ words point toward institutional responsibility; their facial movements do not resolve it.

Duffy’s funding argument also relocates agency. Saying an official cannot act without money may describe a real constraint, but it does not explain who set the budget, which repairs or upgrades went unfunded, or why the system reached the point of a nationwide stoppage. “Money” is not an autonomous force. Elected officials and administration leaders decide what to request, prioritize and defend.

Speculation can protect the powerful

The story’s framing risks misdirecting scrutiny away from the government’s decisions and toward a psychologist’s interpretation of physical behavior. That is convenient for officials even when the resulting coverage sounds accusatory. Readers are invited to wonder what secret lurks behind a lowered gaze instead of examining the administration’s account line by line.

Garrison concluded that there was “very likely” more to the incident than the Trump administration had disclosed. The reporting supplies evidence of tension and apparent disagreement, but it does not establish what that “more” might be. It does not identify a concealed cause, a knowingly false assertion or a specific deceptive act.

The administration still bears responsibility for explaining a nationwide ground stop clearly and consistently. If Mullin and Duffy offered conflicting accounts, shifted responsibility or used budget complaints to evade the immediate question, those are concrete subjects for reporting. Treating stress as proof of dishonesty weakens that scrutiny by replacing accountable statements with an interpretive performance.

The revealing detail is not that two officials blinked under questioning. It is that discussion of a national aviation disruption moved from software rumors to routers, patches, equipment and money without producing a clear account of responsibility. That unresolved chain—not speculative body-language analysis—is where the pressure belongs.

item.title: Historian Jon Meacham warns Trump’s ‘incompetence’ is spooking Americans
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Jon Meacham’s answer was blunt: Americans are unnerved because the Trump administration has put its lack of competence on public display when basic government functions are under strain. Speaking Monday on MS Now’s “Morning Joe,” the historian said people facing crises want experienced officials who know more than they do—not reality television personalities treating public administration as another spectacle. The anxiety Meacham described is not abstract. The discussion centered on failures inv
item.content:encoded:
Jon Meacham’s answer was blunt: Americans are unnerved because the Trump administration has put its lack of competence on public display when basic government functions are under strain. Speaking Monday on MS Now’s “Morning Joe,” the historian said people facing crises want experienced officials who know more than they do—not reality television personalities treating public administration as another spectacle.

The anxiety Meacham described is not abstract. The discussion centered on failures involving the Federal Aviation Administration, grounded planes and a president whose attention, as co-host Joe Scarborough framed it, remained fixed on a grand ballroom while families struggled to afford groceries. Scarborough also pointed to Trump calling affordability a “hoax.” Whatever entertainment value the president extracts from controversy, an aircraft safety system cannot run on provocation.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Government becomes visible when it fails

Meacham argued that the episode exposed the hollowness of decades of rhetoric about government itself being the problem. Americans may disagree over the size and reach of the public sector, but they still expect it to keep planes separated in the sky, food safe and essential infrastructure operating.

The FAA belongs in the same category as traffic signals and utilities, he said: systems whose value rests on their reliability. Passengers do not care about polling when they board an airplane. They need “a basic level of competence.”

That distinction matters because political theater can misdirect responsibility. A failure of government is not evidence that government is inherently incapable. It can also be the foreseeable result of placing incapable people in charge of institutions that require expertise, continuity and disciplined attention. The officials who control appointments, staffing and administrative priorities hold the power; travelers stranded or frightened by the consequences do not.

Meacham did not claim that Democrats would “magically” manage the FAA better. But his insistence that this was not partisan risked sanding down the central fact under discussion: Trump is president, and his administration is responsible for governing. Hypothetical Democratic failure does not distribute accountability for decisions made by the people currently holding federal power.

A presidency organized as spectacle

Scarborough asked whether Americans might again value experience and rationality more than entertainment. He contrasted the recent political era with President Harry Truman’s willingness to retain George Marshall even after Marshall reportedly told Truman that he had not voted for him. The point was not nostalgia for some flawless age. It was that competent government requires leaders capable of valuing expertise above personal loyalty.

Trump has advertised a different model. Meacham recalled Trump saying in 2017 that he wanted a presidency resembling a reality show in which he would “vanquish my opponents.” That conception turns public office into an endless contest of dominance, grievance and audience retention. Agencies then become props, personnel become loyalists or enemies, and administrative failures become opportunities to blame predecessors.

Pointing backward at a former president, Meacham said, does nothing to make government work. It does, however, serve Trump’s preference for keeping public attention fixed on conflict. The controversy is not incidental to the performance; it sustains it. The material consequences—grounded aircraft, disrupted travel and diminished confidence—land elsewhere.

The memory of crisis

Meacham said Friday’s events returned him to the early days of COVID, when Americans looked toward those in authority and wanted reassurance that the people managing the emergency were knowledgeable and capable. As the afternoon unfolded, he said, he was not “filled with confidence, to say the least.”

That comparison identifies the political danger in a government built around personality. Crisis strips away branding. A president can label affordability a hoax, redirect attention toward a ballroom or keep the conversation entertaining, but none of those maneuvers can perform the technical work of aviation safety or restore public confidence in a failing system.

Meacham said the demand for competence had “sure as hell manifested itself in the midterm.” His larger observation was simpler: people expect the public sector to perform certain essential tasks well. Trump may still imagine the presidency as a show about defeating his adversaries. As Meacham put it, “he thinks it’s a reality show, but it’s our reality.” The administration controls the set; the public absorbs the failure.

item.title: ‘Who’s getting fired?’ Trump official cornered on travel chaos live on Fox
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A nationwide aviation shutdown stranded travelers and disrupted thousands of flights on Friday, but the Trump administration’s response was immediate: nobody would lose a job. Appearing on Fox News on Sunday, the official AlterNet identified as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the rare ground stop on an approximately 50-year-old system struggling to operate alongside modern technology. That answer established the administration’s position before the investigation described in
item.content:encoded:
A nationwide aviation shutdown stranded travelers and disrupted thousands of flights on Friday, but the Trump administration’s response was immediate: nobody would lose a job. Appearing on Fox News on Sunday, the official AlterNet identified as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the rare ground stop on an approximately 50-year-old system struggling to operate alongside modern technology.

That answer established the administration’s position before the investigation described in the interview was entirely conclusive. The failure belonged to antiquated equipment; accountability would extend to no one currently in charge.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A system can fail without absolving its stewards

Fox anchor Peter Doocy opened with the blunt question: “Who’s getting fired over this?”

“Oh, I don’t think anybody’s going to get fired over this,” Mullin replied. “This was an issue with the equipment.”

He characterized the infrastructure as “basically an old dial-up system” whose interaction with newer technology had caused problems. That may explain the technical mechanism behind the disruption. It does not answer the institutional question Doocy raised.

Obsolete federal infrastructure does not maintain itself, decide its own budget or set modernization priorities. Officials and lawmakers do. A system can be old enough to have passed through many administrations without making the current administration responsible for five decades of neglect. But the age of the machinery is not a substitute for examining who knew its vulnerabilities, what safeguards existed and why one failure could halt flights nationwide.

Mullin’s refusal to anticipate firings may ultimately prove justified; a technical malfunction does not necessarily establish individual misconduct. But announcing that conclusion while describing the cause with less than complete certainty reverses the usual order of accountability. The personnel verdict arrived before the technical one was final.

Fox offered a foreign villain; Mullin mostly declined

Doocy then steered the interview toward a more politically convenient possibility: a cyberattack. He asked whether a government or hacker might have flooded routers in Arkansas with data and forced the shutdown.

Mullin left a sliver of uncertainty but said the available assessment pointed elsewhere. “I would love to point it at a bad actor because then we know who to go back and punch,” he said. “But the fact is, it isn’t.” He put the likelihood that the aging system caused the failure at 98 percent.

The remark was unusually revealing. A hostile actor would provide a clean antagonist and an uncomplicated show of retaliation. Infrastructure decay offers neither. It instead raises tedious but consequential questions about appropriations, procurement, maintenance and the officials responsible for keeping critical systems functional.

Mullin did not claim certainty beyond what he said investigators had established, and he rejected an unsupported connection between the Federal Aviation Administration failure and a Microsoft outage on consecutive days. When Doocy suggested that viewers understandably suspected “something big,” Mullin acknowledged the conspiracy theories but said there was no basis to connect the incidents.

That was the most responsible part of the exchange. Speculation about hackers may be more dramatic than a legacy-system failure, but drama is not evidence.

The breakdown had consequences; responsibility remains abstract

Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after the nationwide ground stop, according to AlterNet. Travelers experienced the government’s infrastructure problem as missed connections, abandoned plans and airport uncertainty. Yet the official account distributed responsibility in precisely the opposite direction: the public absorbed concrete consequences while the government blamed an impersonal machine.

No evidence in the reported interview establishes that a particular employee deserved dismissal. It does establish that the administration was prepared to rule out that consequence while the cause still carried a stated 2 percent margin of uncertainty. It also shows how easily scrutiny of institutional competence can be diverted into speculation about sabotage.

If the eventual finding remains what Mullin described—a decades-old system failing under the demands of contemporary aviation—the central problem will not be that the machinery was old. It will be that the federal government entrusted nationwide air travel to infrastructure officials knew was old, and its first clear accountability decision after the resulting chaos was that no one would be fired.

item.title: 'Spitting fire': Rick Wilson warns Trump could pay the price for messy fight
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump could pay a political price for the Democratic Senate’s leadership revolt, but only if the party converts its anger into legislative power. Rick Wilson’s warning rests on a specific chain of events that has not yet occurred: Democrats would have to reject Chuck Schumer’s accommodationist instincts, organize a more combative majority and recruit enough Republicans to strip Trump of tariff authority over his veto. That is not a forecast so much as a test. Democrats’ historic midterm g
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump could pay a political price for the Democratic Senate’s leadership revolt, but only if the party converts its anger into legislative power. Rick Wilson’s warning rests on a specific chain of events that has not yet occurred: Democrats would have to reject Chuck Schumer’s accommodationist instincts, organize a more combative majority and recruit enough Republicans to strip Trump of tariff authority over his veto.

That is not a forecast so much as a test. Democrats’ historic midterm gains gave them power; the fight now is over whether their leaders will use it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Schumer’s record is now the issue

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2015, had been widely expected to become majority leader in January. Instead, he faces resistance from voters and incoming senators who regard him as unable or unwilling to mount an effective challenge to Trump.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen has entered the leadership contest after winning support from parts of the Democratic base for opposing Trump’s deportation agenda. Schumer still appears favored, according to AlterNet, but the result was unresolved when Wilson spoke Sunday on Molly Jong-Fast’s “Fast Politics” podcast.

The contest is not merely generational or stylistic. It concerns what Democrats believe their new majority is for. Schumer has already promised to pursue compromise and bipartisanship next year. The voters and senators driving the revolt appear to see that approach as a refusal to recognize the mandate that produced the majority.

Wilson said younger House and Senate members are “spitting fire” because they understand that voters did not send them to Washington for ceremonial collegiality. His language about lawmakers being sent to “burn down this corrupt system” was hyperbolic, but the institutional conflict he described is concrete: new members want investigations, confrontation and rapid policy reversals, while established leaders remain attached to a governing culture built around negotiated routine.

A majority can investigate—or manage decline

Wilson warned Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries against offering limited investigations before returning to minor bipartisan legislation. The crude joke he used to make that point—contrasting timid oversight with a bill on “toilet seat standards”—captured the insurgents’ accusation: Democratic leaders too often treat confrontation with presidential power as an interruption before normal business resumes.

But control of Congress is not symbolic opposition. A majority determines committee leadership, investigative priorities and which bills receive votes. If Democrats confine those powers to gestures, Trump will not “pay the price” for the leadership dispute. He will benefit from it.

That is why the focus on Democratic infighting can itself misdirect. The weaker actors here are not the voters demanding resistance or the incoming senators carrying that demand. The consequential decisions will be made by caucus members choosing their leader—and by whichever leader then controls the Senate’s agenda. A mandate can be diluted without anyone openly repudiating it. Institutional caution, procedural delay and appeals to bipartisanship can accomplish the same result.

Wilson’s tariff scenario remains a wager

Wilson identified tariff authority as the clearest opportunity for a Democratic majority to impose a material defeat on Trump. Congress controls tariffs and taxes, he argued, and could pass legislation revoking the president’s tariff power. He further predicted that enough Republicans would support the measure to override a Trump veto.

That veto-proof coalition is Wilson’s assertion, not a reported fact. So is his claim that ending Trump’s trade policies would cause the economy to rebound and lead voters to credit Democrats. Economic outcomes do not arrive on a commentator’s timetable, and congressional Republicans would have to choose an institutional limit on a Republican president over party discipline.

Still, the proposal exposes the stakes more clearly than the leadership personalities do. Trump’s tariff power depends on authority Congress can contest. If lawmakers believe his trade policy is damaging the economy, they possess tools beyond denunciation. The relevant question is whether they will use those tools when doing so requires a direct fight with the White House and a veto override.

Wilson’s case against Schumer is therefore less about temperament than sequence: win power, act early, produce a visible result. Democrats have completed only the first step. The Senate leadership vote will help determine whether the rest becomes policy or remains podcast bravado.

item.title: Trump strategy unravels in real time — and nobody knows who's in charge
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump is in charge. The disorder surrounding the war with Iran is not evidence that presidential power has disappeared; it is the result of how he is using it. According to AlterNet, Trump has halted a diplomatic initiative, expanded an open-ended military deployment, maintained a blockade without securing commercial shipping and defended a Pentagon chief whose position remains precarious. The administration calls this “strategic waiting.” In practice, it is war policy without a declared
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump is in charge. The disorder surrounding the war with Iran is not evidence that presidential power has disappeared; it is the result of how he is using it. According to AlterNet, Trump has halted a diplomatic initiative, expanded an open-ended military deployment, maintained a blockade without securing commercial shipping and defended a Pentagon chief whose position remains precarious. The administration calls this “strategic waiting.” In practice, it is war policy without a declared destination.

The immediate consequences are already tangible. Another tanker—the fifth in five days—was reportedly burning in the Strait after apparently striking a mine. Fuel prices have not fallen. Iran is rearming and hardening its military infrastructure. American forces are consuming costly interceptor missiles while another carrier group heads toward the region for a deployment military families have been told could last months.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Confusion may describe the experience of soldiers, diplomats, allies and the public. It does not accurately describe the allocation of responsibility.

Trump closes the diplomatic track without opening another

Trump began and abandoned a possible return to negotiations within a week, according to AlterNet. He pulled Vice President JD Vance away from the effort and assigned him instead to investigate alleged fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on social media. “Those days have long since passed.”

That declaration leaves an elementary question unanswered: If there will be no agreement, what ends the war? Trump rejects Iranian demands that the United States leave the Strait and release frozen Iranian assets, but the reporting identifies no alternative mechanism for resolving the conflict. His administration is neither negotiating an exit nor openly committing to the larger campaign that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly wants.

The fraud assignment exposes the domestic political calculation. Vance had blamed adverse midterm results on the Iran war. Trump’s answer was not to define the war’s objective, but to redirect Vance toward Democratic jurisdictions. AlterNet notes that arrests in a Minnesota health-grant fraud case preceded Vance’s involvement and that the reporting provides little basis for treating fraud as a distinctly Democratic phenomenon. Trump has himself pardoned 70 allies and donors implicated in similar offenses.

That maneuver does not settle the corruption question or the Iran war. It changes the subject from presidential responsibility to a familiar partisan target.

A blockade that does not deliver control

Trump claims the United States controls the Strait because it is blocking Iranian vessels. Yet the reported conditions do not resemble control in any useful civilian sense. The extent of international commercial traffic remains disputed, tankers are being damaged, and domestic oil and fuel prices have not abated.

The administration is reinforcing the blockade with another aircraft carrier group, expanding the military commitment while leaving its purpose unclear. Families have reportedly been warned to expect a deployment lasting months. MS NOW has also reported supply shortages affecting the ships, sailors and Marines involved.

This is not merely an incoherent message. It is an asymmetric distribution of risk. Trump retains the authority to escalate or pause; military personnel receive indefinite assignments; merchant crews face hazardous shipping lanes; consumers pay higher fuel costs; and Gulf governments must calculate whether renewed American bombing will bring Iranian retaliation onto their territory.

Secretary of State Mario Rubio’s phrase “strategic waiting” gives the standstill a doctrinal gloss. But waiting is not neutral when the United States is enforcing a blockade, moving additional forces and preserving the option of more bombing. It is continued coercion without a stated route to either victory or withdrawal.

Trump says Gulf allies have asked him to postpone renewed attacks. AlterNet also reports that Trump and Netanyahu had a shouting match over Netanyahu’s demand for further conflict. Trump may be resisting one avenue of escalation, but he has not converted that restraint into a settlement. He has instead left military pressure in place while insisting that no deal is necessary.

Iran’s capacity undercuts the victory story

Trump wants to claim that he personally solved the Iranian nuclear threat and secured the Strait. The military reporting assembled by AlterNet cuts against that account.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Israeli intelligence believes Iran moved thousands of uranium-enrichment centrifuges into tunnels beneath Pickaxe Mountain, potentially preserving the means to rebuild its nuclear program. The Times of Israel reported intelligence estimates that Iran is producing about 50 ballistic missiles each month, roughly half its prewar rate. Iran has also displayed a new underground Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile complex containing ballistic and cruise missiles and their launch systems.

Bloomberg, citing intelligence assessments, reported that Iran retains at least 1,700 ballistic missiles and substantial stocks of cruise missiles and precision-guided bombs. Since joint American-Israeli attacks began on February 28, Iran has reportedly launched more than 4,900 Shahed drones and at least 2,200 ballistic missiles.

Defending against that barrage has imposed its own strain. At least 1,000 Patriot interceptors have reportedly been expended against attacks on American and allied targets. Each costs about $4 million, while annual production is approximately 650. Iran, meanwhile, says it will move missile and drone production underground.

Those figures do not establish that Tehran can achieve its objectives, but they do show why Trump’s suggestion in a recent “60 Minutes” interview that Iran’s nuclear capability no longer concerns him cannot substitute for a strategy. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said this week that Tehran would not surrender any enriched nuclear material and that no negotiations with Washington were underway.

If preventing Iranian nuclear development was the stated reason for war, dismissing the issue while Iran buries centrifuges deeper underground is not resolution. It is an attempt to declare the original problem solved before the available intelligence supports the claim.

Domestic weakness is shaping foreign policy

Trump’s hesitation comes amid anti-war pressure and damaging midterm results. A new Democratic majority is due to take control of both chambers of Congress in January and, according to AlterNet, intends to oppose further war funding and demand compliance with the War Powers Act.

That looming confrontation appears to be driving decisions elsewhere. Trump announced that $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel would end by year’s close, a move AlterNet interprets as an effort to act before Congress forces the issue. He is also defending Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while reportedly discussing replacements. An impeachment vote against Hegseth failed to advance only after several opposition lawmakers were caught in traffic.

The Pentagon therefore faces a prolonged deployment under a secretary whose tenure is in doubt, serving a president who has rejected negotiations without defining the conditions for ending hostilities. Calling that arrangement a chain of command does not make it a coherent policy.

Democrats, for their part, are described as having little developed plan beyond invoking war-powers restrictions and threatening to withhold money. Those are substantial congressional powers, not cosmetic objections. But blocking an undefined war is not the same as presenting a workable diplomatic settlement.

Trump’s actual strategy appears designed to preserve his freedom of action through the transition: keep the blockade, add forces, decline negotiations, avoid immediate bombing and insist that the main objectives have already been achieved. It allows him to postpone a choice while others absorb the costs.

Even the administration’s proposed purchase of Russian diesel has stalled. Multiple outlets report that American ports, refineries and terminal operators are avoiding the shipments despite a temporary White House sanctions waiver, citing legal and reputational risks. New Jersey officials have said unloading the fuel would violate the law. Tankers are reportedly stranded.

That is the pattern running through the episode: presidential announcements collide with military capacity, commercial caution, allied resistance, congressional power and conditions on the ground. Nobody may know what Trump will decide next. But there is no mystery about who constructed the standstill or who still possesses the authority to end it.

item.title: The 2 words that made the FAA ground stop sound like a cover-up
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The two words were “nothing nefarious.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin repeated them after the Federal Aviation Administration halted all domestic flights on Nov. 13, 2026, amid reported failures in aging air-traffic communications equipment. item.content:encoded:
The two words were “nothing nefarious.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin repeated them after the Federal Aviation Administration halted all domestic flights on Nov. 13, 2026, amid reported failures in aging air-traffic communications equipment. The phrase was supposed to reassure thousands of stranded travelers. Instead, it introduced the possibility of sabotage or a cyberattack before the administration had publicly explained the hardware failure it said caused the shutdown.

That verbal blunder, however, was not the central failure. A nationwide ground stop had exposed the fragility of infrastructure responsible for keeping aircraft safely separated, and administration officials spent part of their response making a funding argument without adequately answering the immediate question: What had failed, what had been repaired, and why should passengers believe the system was safe again?

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An assurance that manufactured suspicion

Shannon A. Bowen, a University of South Carolina crisis-communications scholar, told The Conversation that officials initially followed a basic rule of emergency communication: speak quickly and disclose what is known before speculation fills the vacuum.

Mullin then created the speculation himself.

By repeatedly insisting that there was “nothing nefarious” involved, he made nefarious activity a national talking point. Bowen said officials would have been better served by stating the affirmative case they claimed to possess: evidence indicated a hardware failure, not a cyberattack. That formulation would have identified the reported cause and excluded an alternative. Mullin’s wording did the reverse, asking the public to trust a denial untethered from a clear explanation.

Bowen argued that the phrase made the episode sound suspicious even if the only misconduct at issue was mismanagement of the routers behind the air-traffic system. The distinction matters. There is no basis in the supplied reporting to conclude that the shutdown concealed an attack. There is ample reason to scrutinize why officials foregrounded an unnamed menace while leaving basic operational questions unresolved.

The cover-up atmosphere came from the administration’s communication, not reported evidence of a cover-up.

The machinery failed; the briefing shifted to money

At a later appearance, Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy disclosed what they knew and fielded questions, Bowen said. But they also appeared to minimize the disruption and moved into a political case for more infrastructure funding.

The need described was substantial: officials had been seeking at least $30 billion to repair the air-traffic control system. Yet invoking that long-term price tag did not tell stranded passengers what the government was doing that day, whether the defective equipment had been restored, or whether flights then in the air were safer than those operating immediately before the shutdown.

Those were not public-relations niceties. They went to the government’s core responsibility in the crisis. The FAA controls the national airspace; cabinet officials control the federal account of what happened. Travelers do not have access to the routers, the failure logs or the remediation plan. When officials substitute assurances and budget advocacy for concrete operational information, they exploit an information imbalance created by their own institutional power.

Bowen also questioned why malfunctioning equipment could not have been restarted during a less disruptive period if overloaded routers were the problem. She cited a reported 17 failures among 22 routers and asked whether officials could have restricted the shutdown to affected airports instead of stopping domestic flights nationwide. The interview did not establish that either alternative was technically feasible, but the questions expose the gap the administration needed to address: why this remedy, at this scale, at this time?

A foreseeable crisis in an aging system

The administration could not plausibly present the breakdown as an unimaginable bolt from the sky. Bowen pointed to another air-traffic-related ground stop roughly three years earlier, describing it as a warning of larger failures to come.

Duffy reinforced that assessment. Because of the infrastructure’s condition, he said on Nov. 13, “you will have more” ground stoppages. That is a remarkable admission from the official overseeing transportation: nationwide aviation disruption is no longer merely a past failure to explain but a recurring consequence the government expects.

Officials are entitled to argue that Congress must finance repairs. They are not entitled to let that argument obscure executive responsibility for contingency planning, airline coordination and honest warnings to passengers. Bowen suggested advance public notices when a ground stop is under consideration, along with earlier consultation with airlines about reducing the harm. Those measures would not replace modern equipment, but they could keep travelers from arriving at airports for flights the government may prevent from departing.

The disruption reached well beyond business travel. Athletic teams and other groups were stranded; the University of South Carolina marching band was caught in the shutdown, though the school’s football team had already departed. Such examples illustrate the reach of the failure, but the stakes are larger than disrupted schedules. A communications breakdown serious enough to empty the domestic sky is an emergency involving the basic reliability of national infrastructure.

The administration’s most revealing message therefore did not come from Mullin’s clumsy denial. It came from Duffy’s forecast. “Nothing nefarious” may have made the briefing sound like concealment, but “you will have more” described the material consequence: officials expect the system to fail again.

item.title: Not in My Backyard: How Homeowners Hijacked the Right to Build
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: From San Francisco to London, the housing crisis isn’t simply a failure to build. item.content:encoded:
From San Francisco to London, the housing crisis isn’t simply a failure to build. It’s what happens when the people who already have homes are given the political power to keep everyone else out.

Nine Years. Zero Apartments. One Very Important Parking Lot.

In 2017, a developer proposed something apparently outrageous in San Francisco: replacing a downtown parking lot with 495 apartments.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Not demolishing a historic landmark. Not paving over a protected forest. Not displacing hundreds of existing families.

A parking lot.

The property, at 469 Stevenson Street, was supposed to become a 27-story residential tower, complete with affordable housing. The San Francisco Planning Commission approved the project in 2021.

Then came the neighborhood opposition.

A local group appealed the decision. The Board of Supervisors voted 8–3 to overturn the project's environmental certification, citing concerns including shadows on a nearby plaza and potential effects on neighborhood rents.

Apparently, San Francisco had discovered a radical new principle of urban planning:

If housing is too expensive, the solution is to prevent people from building more of it.

The State of California intervened, investigating whether the city's actions violated state housing law. The project was approved again in 2023.

And as of March 2026?

Still a parking lot.

The developer was requesting an extension of its approvals through 2029, citing challenging market conditions and rising construction costs.

Nine years of planning, approvals, appeals, reconsiderations, and political obstruction, and San Francisco had managed to preserve one of its most precious urban resources:

A place to park cars.

Meanwhile, hundreds of potential households remained without the apartments that could have stood there.

Welcome to the wonderful world of NIMBYism.

Not in My Backyard — But Especially Not Near My Property Value

NIMBY stands for “Not In My Backyard,” a term describing people who oppose developments near their homes even when they acknowledge that those developments may be needed elsewhere.

The phenomenon is not exclusive to homeowners, nor is every objection to development illegitimate.

But when housing construction threatens perceived neighborhood exclusivity, the familiar arguments emerge.

The building is too tall. It will create shadows. Traffic will get worse. Parking will become difficult. The neighborhood will lose its character.

And frequently lurking beneath those objections is another concern:

What will happen to my property's value?

Let's be clear about something.

Owning a home gives you property rights. It does not give you ownership of the entire neighborhood.

You are entitled to protection against dangerous construction, unlawful encroachment, and demonstrable damage to your property.

You are not automatically entitled to an unobstructed view forever, unlimited street parking, or a neighborhood frozen at the precise moment you purchased your house.

And you certainly shouldn't be entitled to prevent hundreds of other people from finding housing merely because their arrival might inconvenience you.

That's not the defense of private property.

That's the appropriation of everyone else's property rights for your personal benefit.

It's like an HOA, except considerably worse.

An HOA might fine you because your lawn is two inches too tall.

An organized NIMBY movement can help ensure that hundreds of families never have a lawn, an apartment, or even a front door in the first place.

And the truly remarkable part is that the political system often treats this as responsible civic engagement.

The People Who Don't Live There Don't Get a Vote

Here is the structural defect that makes NIMBYism so effective.

Existing homeowners vote.

They attend neighborhood meetings. They contact elected officials. They organize opposition campaigns. They challenge planning decisions.

But the people who would eventually live in those 495 apartments?

They don't live there yet.

They may be young professionals who cannot afford to move into the city. Teachers commuting from distant communities. Healthcare workers spending hours in traffic. Families sharing overcrowded housing because rents are prohibitive.

Some may already live in San Francisco but desperately need somewhere more suitable.

They are real people with real housing needs.

Yet they are often invisible in the local political process.

The people potentially inconvenienced by new construction are identifiable, organized, and politically influential.

The people who would benefit from it are dispersed, frequently unknown, and poorly represented.

The people who already have housing get to help decide whether the people who need housing will ever get any.

And politicians, naturally, respond to the voters standing in front of them.

This is how a legitimate democratic process can become a mechanism of exclusion.

Not because democracy itself is defective, but because the political constituency affected by a decision is larger than the constituency allowed meaningful influence over it.

The people excluded from a city by its housing policies are still affected by those policies.

They just don't get much of a say.

London: NIMBYism with a British Accent

Perhaps this is simply an American pathology?

Unfortunately, no.

Consider London.

Like San Francisco, London is an economically important city with enormous housing demand and punishing housing costs.

England's planning system provides statutory decision periods of eight weeks for ordinary applications and thirteen weeks for major developments, subject to exceptions and agreed extensions.

Sounds reasonable.

Until we remember that statutory deadlines and actual development timelines are not the same thing.

Local councils consult residents, consider objections, and sometimes refer controversial projects to elected planning committees.

Shadows, traffic, parking, privacy, and neighborhood appearance can all be legitimate planning considerations.

One important distinction, however, is that British planning guidance does not treat a reduction in neighboring property values as a legitimate reason to refuse permission.

Nor do neighbors ordinarily have a direct right to appeal an approval through the planning appeals system. Legal challenges generally concern whether the decision was lawful.

That's an improvement over a system where political opposition can repeatedly reopen approved projects.

Yet London still struggles to deliver enough housing.

Why?

Because even without an ordinary third-party appeal, politically sensitive planning decisions can become slow, contentious, and expensive.

Developers face uncertainty. Local councils face organized opposition. Politicians face homeowners who know exactly whom to blame if something changes in their neighborhood.

Different mechanisms.

Familiar outcome.

Paris: You Can Challenge the Law, Not Simply Your Neighbor's Existence

France offers another model.

In Paris, building projects generally require a permis de construire, assessed against applicable planning rules, building requirements, and heritage protections.

Paris is hardly a paradise of deregulation. Its historical architecture is extensively protected, and construction can be extraordinarily complicated.

However, the system makes an important distinction.

A neighbor who believes a permit is unlawful can challenge it through administrative procedures and the courts. The ordinary period for a third-party legal challenge is two months from proper public display of the authorization.

But an objection must rest on a legally recognized basis.

“I don't want those people living near me” is not, by itself, a planning-law argument.

Neither is “I liked my neighborhood better before someone bought the empty lot.”

France still allows development disputes, and legal challenges can be costly. But the governing principle is worth examining:

The question is whether construction complies with the law, not whether its neighbors find it socially acceptable.

That difference matters.

Berlin: There Is a Rule for That

Germany provides an especially revealing contrast.

Berlin has several construction authorization procedures, including an exemption mechanism called Genehmigungsfreistellung.

For qualifying projects that comply with the applicable development plan and other requirements, construction can generally proceed after one month following submission of complete documentation, provided the authorities don't intervene.

Larger or more complicated developments may require ordinary or simplified permits, technical reviews, and additional approvals.

A 27-story tower does not magically receive approval in thirty days simply because it is located in Germany.

But the underlying philosophy is different.

If a project qualifies under an established set of rules, those rules can provide a relatively predictable path forward.

Neighbors may challenge violations of legally protected interests. They do not possess a general entitlement to stop lawful construction simply because they dislike additional housing.

Germany certainly has housing problems of its own, including high construction costs, financing difficulties, and bureaucratic delays.

The lesson isn't that German bureaucracy is wonderful.

The lesson is that predictable rules are preferable to perpetual political renegotiation.

A developer should be able to determine what is legally permitted before spending years attempting to build it.

And a neighbor's personal preferences should not acquire the force of law merely because that neighbor is loud enough.

Brazil: The City Hall, the Permit, and the Absence of a Neighborhood Referendum

Now consider a system familiar to many Brazilians.

In municipalities such as Santo André, in metropolitan São Paulo, the ordinary approach is to submit construction plans to the municipal authorities for evaluation under the applicable building code, zoning rules, and land-use regulations.

Santo André even operates an electronic licensing system called Obra Fácil.

For straightforward projects, the process can be relatively quick, although approval times vary considerably with complexity. Large developments, environmental restrictions, and neighborhood-impact requirements can introduce additional scrutiny.

Brazilian bureaucracy can be maddening. Nobody seriously needs to be told otherwise.

But there is an important distinction between obtaining municipal approval and asking the neighborhood for permission.

For an ordinary, legally compliant project, the municipality generally doesn't conduct a popularity contest among neighboring homeowners.

The property owner submits the required documentation. The government evaluates the proposed construction.

If the project satisfies the applicable requirements, it can be authorized.

Neighbors retain legal protections against violations and harmful activities. Major developments can require public-impact assessments and consultation.

But disliking a proposal is not ordinarily sufficient to stop it.

Imagine having to ask everyone on your street whether you may build a house on land you already own.

And then imagine that, even after city hall approves it, a neighborhood association can drag the decision back into political proceedings because your house might cast a shadow across someone's favorite afternoon reading spot.

That is the absurdity San Francisco has repeatedly demonstrated.

China: The Opposite Extreme

China provides a very different warning.

For decades, Chinese local governments had strong incentives to expand construction and infrastructure investment.

The results were extraordinary.

Entire districts, vast transportation networks, and enormous residential complexes appeared at a pace difficult to imagine in most Western cities.

Sometimes, however, China built considerably more than local demand could immediately absorb.

Kangbashi, in Inner Mongolia, became internationally famous as a supposed ghost city.

Planned for approximately 300,000 residents, it had around 119,000 in the 2020 census.

Empty residential towers and sprawling streets make compelling television.

But the comparison raises a question that Western housing debates often ignore.

Why is excess housing considered an obvious planning failure, while chronic housing shortages are treated as an unavoidable fact of life?

Overbuilding can be economically disastrous, especially when financed through unsustainable debt or driven by speculative demand.

China's property-sector problems are substantial, and nobody should mistake government-directed construction for a universally successful model.

But a city can also suffer from underbuilding.

One system may create buildings without sufficient residents.

Another may have residents desperately seeking buildings that powerful interests won't allow to exist.

Neither represents sound planning.

Yet only one shortage is routinely defended as protecting neighborhood character.

The Economics NIMBYs Would Rather Ignore

There is another problem with the claim that building more apartments will necessarily make housing less affordable.

It conflicts with a substantial body of economic research.

A 2024 review by Vicki Been, Ingrid Gould Ellen, and Katherine O'Regan, published in Housing Policy Debate, examined recent research into housing supply and rental costs.

The authors found that increasing housing supply generally reduces rents or slows their growth at the regional level, with some studies identifying similar effects in surrounding neighborhoods.

A separate study by Andreas Mense, published in 2025 in the Journal of Political Economy Macroeconomics, found that new housing supply can reduce rents across different market segments.

Why?

Because housing markets are interconnected.

When someone moves into a new apartment, they often leave another dwelling available. Someone else moves into that one, potentially freeing another.

New housing creates chains of moves that can increase availability beyond the newly constructed building itself.

Of course, merely approving expensive luxury apartments will not magically provide decent housing for everyone.

Cities need genuinely affordable housing, subsidized construction, preservation of existing low-cost units, and protections against displacement.

But none of those objectives is served by preventing housing construction altogether.

And here's the particularly ugly part of the 469 Stevenson controversy.

The proposed development included affordable apartments.

The 2023 approval provided for 73 affordable units on-site.

The 2026 extension request sought to reduce the on-site affordable share from 19% to 15%, an unfortunate development that underscores how financial pressures can weaken affordability commitments.

That doesn't mean every dollar of increased construction cost can be attributed to NIMBY opposition. Inflation, financing conditions, labor, and materials all affect projects.

But prolonged political obstruction certainly doesn't make construction cheaper.

And when a development becomes financially impossible, the city doesn't get more affordable homes.

It gets nothing.

Or, in this case, a parking lot.

When NIMBYism Becomes the Law

There is something even more outrageous than homeowners organizing to stop apartment buildings from being constructed.

In much of the United States, they don't even need to organize.

The law has already prohibited the apartments.

Welcome to exclusionary zoning, one of the most effective mechanisms ever devised for creating housing scarcity while pretending to regulate urban development.

Consider Los Angeles.

Under its traditional R1 residential zoning, a property owner is generally permitted to build a single-family house, subject to applicable exceptions. A conventional apartment building, however, is not ordinarily permitted in that same zone.

And the restrictions don't end there.

The standard minimum lot size is 5,000 square feet.

That's approximately 465 square meters.

Imagine owning a perfectly suitable piece of land in a city suffering from a housing shortage, wanting to construct a modest four-unit apartment building, and being told that the law reserves your property primarily for one detached house.

Not because the apartment building would be structurally unsound.

Not because the land is environmentally protected.

Not because the infrastructure cannot accommodate additional residents.

But because the zoning designation says so.

California has begun loosening these restrictions. Since 2022, Senate Bill 9 has permitted qualifying two-unit developments and lot splits in single-family zones, with subsequent amendments expanding and refining the framework.

San Francisco has also begun dismantling some of its restrictions. Its Family Zoning Plan, effective January 2026, allows greater density and taller buildings in designated areas, especially along commercial and transit corridors.

These are welcome changes.

But consider what they reveal.

For decades, American cities legally prohibited people from building the very housing those cities desperately needed.

And this wasn't merely an unfortunate consequence of otherwise sensible regulations.

The historical record is considerably uglier.

In 1917, the United States Supreme Court struck down explicit racial residential segregation ordinances in Buchanan v. Warley.

But racial and economic exclusion did not disappear.

Instead, zoning restrictions became an alternative means of controlling who could afford to live in particular neighborhoods.

Minimum lot sizes. Single-family-only districts. Restrictions on apartments. Minimum building dimensions. Requirements that increased construction costs.

The language changed.

The exclusion continued.

In 1926, the Supreme Court upheld municipal zoning authority in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., helping establish the legal foundation for the restrictive residential zoning that spread throughout the country.

And the consequences were enormous.

A 2024 study from the University of California, Berkeley found that approximately 82% of California's residential land within incorporated jurisdictions was zoned exclusively for single-family housing under the zoning rules examined.

Eighty-two percent.

In a state synonymous with astronomical housing prices, vast portions of residential land were legally reserved for the least space-efficient conventional housing arrangement.

Think about the implications.

You cannot construct enough apartments because the zoning doesn't permit them.

You cannot easily change the zoning because existing residents oppose increased density.

You cannot accommodate the population without expanding outward, increasing commuting distances, infrastructure costs, and dependence on cars.

And when housing prices inevitably soar, politicians solemnly announce that the city is experiencing a housing crisis.

As though the shortage had fallen from the sky.

They didn't merely fail to build enough housing. They wrote laws restricting how much housing could be built.

Now, not every zoning restriction is illegitimate.

Separating hazardous industrial operations from residential neighborhoods is sensible. Protecting floodplains, ensuring structural safety, and maintaining adequate infrastructure are essential government responsibilities.

But preventing a duplex, triplex, or modest apartment building from existing in a residential neighborhood simply because it contains multiple households?

That deserves a much better justification than preserving neighborhood character.

Because “neighborhood character” has an extraordinarily convenient habit of meaning whatever the existing homeowners want it to mean.

And historically, those preferences have not always been innocent.

The particularly bitter irony is that many of the same political voices celebrating property rights and opposing government interference have little objection to government prohibiting another property owner from constructing additional homes.

Apparently, freedom extends all the way to the property line.

And then it becomes someone else's problem.

NIMBYism is bad enough when it takes the form of a neighborhood protest.

It is considerably worse when it has been written into the municipal code.

At that point, exclusion doesn't need angry homeowners standing outside city hall.

It has the force of law.

The Property-Rights Hypocrisy

This is where the American contradiction becomes almost comical.

The United States has an extensive political tradition celebrating private property, individual liberty, and limited government interference.

Politicians regularly lecture the public about the sanctity of ownership.

Until someone wants to build apartments.

Suddenly, private property is everyone's business.

The height of the building. The appearance of its exterior. The number of apartments. The hypothetical impact on somebody else's investment.

And the neighbors who demand government intervention to prevent construction may be the same people who insist that government should stay out of private affairs.

Apparently, property rights are sacred only when they belong to people who already own the surrounding property.

This is not an argument for abolishing zoning, environmental protections, or building standards.

Those rules exist for legitimate reasons.

The public has every right to demand structurally safe buildings, adequate infrastructure, environmental safeguards, and compliance with democratically adopted planning requirements.

But there is a world of difference between enforcing rules and allowing organized groups to manipulate those rules into instruments of exclusion.

A property right that depends on the political approval of every nearby property owner is not much of a right at all.

And a housing policy designed around preserving the comfort of existing homeowners is not a housing policy.

It's an exclusion policy.

Democracy Is Not a Neighborhood Veto

Supporters of extensive neighborhood participation often invoke democracy.

Residents deserve a voice, they argue.

And they do.

But having a voice is not the same as possessing a veto.

A democratic government must consider the interests of everyone affected by its decisions, including people who are not organized into neighborhood associations.

Including renters.

Including future residents.

Including workers who commute from miles away because they cannot afford to live near their jobs.

Including young adults who cannot establish independent households.

Including families who must choose between overcrowding and financial ruin.

When the political process repeatedly elevates the preferences of established homeowners over the housing needs of everyone else, it ceases to function as balanced public planning.

It becomes an institution for protecting incumbents.

And its consequences are not abstract.

Housing shortages increase financial pressure, constrain labor mobility, worsen long-distance commuting, and prevent people from living near employment and essential services.

The price of preserving one neighborhood's preferred appearance is distributed across people who may never have visited that neighborhood at all.

That's the part missing from so many local planning meetings.

The people denied housing don't disappear.

They move farther away, pay more, crowd together, postpone major life decisions, or leave the region entirely.

The costs are real.

They simply don't appear on the neighborhood association's balance sheet.

Stop Giving Parking Lots More Rights Than People

The solution is not to eliminate planning.

It's to restore its proper purpose.

Establish sensible zoning laws. Allow enough density to meet actual housing demand. Require appropriate environmental and safety protections. Build and subsidize affordable housing. Protect existing residents from genuine displacement.

And then, when a project complies with the rules, allow it to be built.

Public objections should be evaluated against identifiable legal and material concerns, not treated as an inexhaustible source of political delay.

Procedures should have meaningful deadlines. Unnecessary duplication should be eliminated. Approval should mean something.

Most importantly, governments should stop pretending that protecting the preferences of existing property owners is the same thing as protecting the public interest.

Sometimes those interests align.

Sometimes they don't.

And when hundreds of people need homes while a politically influential minority wants to preserve a parking lot, public officials should be capable of recognizing the difference.

San Francisco's 469 Stevenson Street development is not merely a story about one failed construction timetable.

It is a demonstration of how a city can acknowledge a housing crisis, approve a solution, obstruct that solution, approve it again, and then watch the economics of construction deteriorate while nothing gets built.

All while claiming to care deeply about housing affordability.

Nine years.

Nearly 500 proposed apartments.

A city desperate for housing.

And the parking lot survives.

The housing crisis wasn't inevitable. The obstruction was a choice.

And the people making that choice already had somewhere to live.

item.title: RFK Jr. and the Dangerous Arrogance of Not Knowing What You’re Doing
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: How America’s Health Secretary turned public-health prevention into a budgetary inconvenience — and why Senator Raphael Warnock’s interrogation exposed something more troubling than ignorance.
